problem: Existing navigation benchmarks (R2R, REVERIE, ObjectNav) were built for supervised agents and report only final success rates, so they say little about whether MLLMs truly understand navigation behavior. They also treat all episodes as equally difficult and have no real-world transfer path.
motivation: MLLMs generalize well on static vision-language tasks, but it is unclear whether they can understand and act in embodied environments. Humans first comprehend a navigation task and then execute it, so a diagnostic benchmark should probe both comprehension and step-by-step execution, with difficulty stratification.
key_idea: NavBench is a zero-shot MLLM navigation benchmark that pairs three comprehension probes (global instruction alignment, temporal progress estimation, local observation-action reasoning) with difficulty-stratified step-by-step execution (easy/medium/hard by spatial, cognitive and execution complexity), plus a real-robot deployment pipeline.
insight: Comprehension and execution scores are correlated (GPT-4o best on both; weaker models mostly succeed only on easy episodes). Temporal reasoning is the persistent weakness: Progress Estimation is low for nearly all models and the shuffled-sub-instruction distractors in Global Alignment are poorly handled. Adding map connectivity text helps GPT-4o most at medium difficulty (+4.51 avg), and manual error analysis links failures to poor progress estimation (failure to stop).
method: Global Instruction Alignment: 1,200 multiple-choice items; each has a panoramic trajectory and 5 candidate instructions (1 GT + 4 distractors from basic random, direction replacement, object replacement, shuffled sub-instructions).
Temporal Progress Estimation: 1,000 items; the trajectory is truncated at sub-instruction boundaries (using FGR2R alignments) and the model predicts the index of the last completed sub-instruction.
Local Observation-Action Reasoning: 1,000 items (500 Future-Observation Prediction, 500 Future-Action Prediction) with distractors from nearby views or similar actions.

Navigation Execution: 432 episodes over 72 Matterport3D scenes; at each step the MLLM gets the panorama, the instruction, candidate navigable viewpoints and optional history, and selects the next viewpoint (SR within 3 m, SPL).

Difficulty scoring: composite spatial (path length, turn-angle std, elevation, area), cognitive (instruction length, verbs, spatial terms, landmarks, clauses) and execution (steps, turns, floor change, decision points) scores are log-normalized to 1-9 and validated by human ratings, then binned into easy (1-3), medium (4-6) and hard (7-9).

Real-world pipeline: a waypoint predictor from RGB-D proposes candidates, an MLLM selects the most goal-aligned waypoint, and a low-level controller drives a dual-arm wheeled robot with a RealSense D435.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, InternVL2.5-2B/8B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Llama3.2-Vision-11B (all frozen, zero-shot)
setting.model_size: 2B-11B for open-source models; GPT-4o is proprietary
setting.observation: panoramic RGB and single-view RGB from Matterport3D; RGB-D on the real robot
setting.action_space: discrete navigable-viewpoint selection in simulation; predicted waypoints converted to low-level control on the real robot
setting.privileged: none (the map-connectivity text is only an optional ablation)

Only a few representative rows are listed; Table 1 has more models (GPT-4o-mini, InternVL2.5, LLaVA-OV, Llama3.2-V, etc.). Per-distractor and local-subtask results appear only in figures. The text and table disagree on the medium-difficulty map gain (text says +4.86 SR; the table shows +4.86 SR and +4.51 avg).
results: GPT-4o is best overall (comprehension avg 53.34, execution avg 41.33), followed by the best open-source model Qwen2.5-VL-7B (45.26 / 21.77), which is close to GPT-4o-mini (46.42 / 27.99). Humans reach 84.11 comprehension and 81.59 execution on the tiny subset, so a large gap remains. Real-robot pilot on 10 cases: GPT-4o 60% SR, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 40%.
limitations: Execution uses viewpoint selection in Matterport3D rather than low-level control, and the difficulty weights are set empirically.
The real-world validation is a small pilot (10 cases per model) in a controlled lab.
Only a handful of MLLMs are evaluated, with no fine-tuned or specialist navigation models.
